newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Colombo port prepares to compete with P&O.
newsitem.headline: Colombo port prepares to compete with P&O.

text.p: Colombo port will soon set up a company to handle transshipment business and compete with Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co (P&O) which is to lease one of its container terminals, officials said on Sunday.

"We will float a limited liability company wholly owned by the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA) to operate the Jaye container terminals and conventional cargo berths," said Ranjit Wickramasinghe, chairman of the SLPA which runs the port.
"In order to face competition with P&O we have to have the necessary flexibility and also need a level playing field for competition," he told Reuters.
Britain's P&O is currently holding talks with the SLPA on a 30-year lease of Colombo port's Queen Elizabeth Quay container terminal.

The project, on a build, operate and transfer basis, will be implemented by South Asia Gateway Terminals (SAGT), a venture bewteen P&O Navigation Australia, P&O Containers of Britain, Sri Lankan conglomerate John Keells Holdings Ltd and the SLPA.

Port officials said the new company to be set up under the SLPA will enjoy the same fiscal incentives, like duty free imports and exemption from inland revenue and exchange controls, that will be given to SAGT.
Wickramasinghe also said that the SLPA plans to raise navigation and stevedore tariffs by April 1 to meet rising costs.
"We're proposing to increase tariffs in those areas which have not been increased for the last several years," he said.
Port officials said navigation tariffs will rise by 19-25 percent and stevedore charges by 10 percent.
"We have not revised these rates since 1982 -- for nearly 15 years," said a senior port official who declined to be identified.
"In the meantime we have spent huge sums of money on tugs and dredging and improving the port's infrastructure. We cannot function like this without raising charges," he added.
In June 1995, the port increased transshipment tariffs by 20 percent.
Colombo port, south Asia's transshipment hub, last year handled almost 1.4 million containers, up 29 percent from 1995, and is seen nearing its capacity of 1.6 million units this year.

Transshipment, which occurs when a vessel discharges cargo at an intermediate port and the goods are unloaded to another ship bound for the final destination, accounts for about 70 percent of the port's throughput.
